title: SDK Flow-Control Contract for Streaming and Paged Endpoints (Python / TS / Go)
creator: Aisha Patel
description: This PRD defines a cross-language client contract for flow control, backpressure, pagination, and retry semantics across Redwood SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Go). The goal is to provide predictable behavior for streaming and paged endpoints so product teams can rely on consistent latency, replayability, and upgrade paths. This ticket focuses on the contract (APIs, expected semantics, and interop tests); separate implementation tickets will exist per-language. The document includes acceptance criteria, compatibility rules, testing strategy, and a phased rollout plan.
goals: Define a unified stream envelope and control signals that all SDKs implement
Specify pagination cursor semantics and idempotency guarantees for paged endpoints
Standardize retryable vs non-retryable errors and backoff defaults across SDKs
Provide a downgrade/compatibility policy so new SDKs interoperate with older runtimes
Create a cross-language integration test suite for streaming, pagination, and retry behaviors
non_goals: Implementing language SDK changes (this ticket is the product spec)
Changing billing or token accounting semantics
scope_changes: Scope initially included only streaming envelopes; expanded to include paged endpoints after PM/Eng alignment on 2026-03-12
Added explicit migration guidance for customers using legacy cursor tokens
Included Go channel-based API requirements following feedback from infra teams
requirements: Streaming envelope: each chunk must be a JSON object with keys: 'data' (string|object), 'seq' (monotonic increasing integer per-stream), 'eos' (boolean) and optional 'meta' (map) for signals. SDKs must surface 'seq' and 'eos' to callers.

Backpressure controls: SDKs must expose an opt-in flow control API. Defaults: max_inflight=8, read_window=65536 bytes. Languages may expose idiomatic primitives (async iterator buffer size for Python/TS; buffered channel for Go).

Cancellation/Abort: all streaming APIs must accept a cancellation token / AbortSignal. On cancel, SDK must: stop reading, close underlying connection if no other streams use it, and surface a CancelledError with partial progress metadata.

Pagination contract: cursor tokens are opaque but stable; servers must accept previous cursors for at least 7 days. Cursors must encode position + optional checksum. Clients should treat cursors as opaque strings; provide helpers to detect truncated results.

Idempotency: page fetches with a given cursor should be retryable if server responds with transient error (5xx, 429 with 'Retry-After'). Non-retryable errors include validation (4xx excluding 429) and auth failures.

Retries: default retry policy is exponential backoff with jitter; max_attempts=3 for idempotent ops (pagination fetches) and 1 for non-idempotent streaming append actions. SDKs must surface retry hooks so applications can instrument or override behavior.

Compatibility: SDKs must support a graceful degradation mode when connecting to older servers that lack 'seq' or 'eos' fields. In that case, the SDK should synthesize monotonic seq numbers and set eos when connection closes, but log a warning to the console/tracer.

Diagnostics: every SDK call related to streaming/pagination must attach structured telemetry: operation, model, backend_version, seq/offset when available. Telemetry must be configurable to PII-safe level by the application.
Cross-language parity: public surface area should be idiomatic per language but offer equivalent capabilities. Example: Python async iterator vs TS AsyncIterable vs Go channel + context-based cancel.
Error envelopes: standardize on an error envelope with 'code' (string), 'message' (string), 'retriable' (boolean), and optional 'retry_after' (seconds)
acceptance_criteria: Spec reviewed and signed off by Engineering leads for Python/TS/Go, SDK owners, and Security
Cross-language interop test suite exists and passes against both new runtime (feature flags enabled) and existing runtime (feature flags disabled)
SDK API doc pages updated with usage examples: streaming backpressure, cancel patterns, paged iterators, and migration notes
End-to-end demo app that exercises a long-running streaming call under simulated network contention and shows stable behavior
Performance targets: default streaming latency overhead introduced by SDK must be < 5ms median per-chunk for small chunks (<1KB) under normal CPU load
Compatibility tests: older clients + new servers and new clients + older servers must not cause data loss; synthesized seq/eos behavior validated
api_surface_changes: Python: streaming endpoint returns an AsyncIterable[StreamChunk] with optional 'control' object exposing pause/resume and current_inflight()
TypeScript: AsyncIterable<StreamChunk> plus optional FlowController returned from stream() call for manual window adjustments
Go: func Stream(ctx context.Context, params) (chan StreamChunk, CancelFunc) where StreamChunk includes Seq and EOS flags
Pagination: list() helpers return a Pager object with next() and iter() helpers in all languages; pager exposes current_cursor and is_retryable() helper
compatibility_policy: Minor SDK releases must be backwards compatible with server endpoints for 12 months unless a security or compliance issue demands immediate change
Servers may introduce additional optional fields in stream envelopes; SDKs must ignore unknown fields
When a breaking change is required, a 3-month deprecation window is required with console-level telemetry and an automatic opt-in feature flag for early adopters
Clients connecting to legacy servers will use synthesized seq/eos and log a single warning per process to avoid noise
migration_guide: For customers using legacy cursor tokens, provide a migration script that exchanges legacy tokens for stable v2 cursors using a server-side migration endpoint
Document sample code for moving from callback-based streaming to AsyncIterator-based consumption in each SDK
Provide a compatibility shim package for TS that polyfills FlowController APIs for older SDK consumers during transition
testing_plan: Unit tests for envelope parsing, seq monotonicity, eos behavior, and synthesized fallbacks
Integration tests: run cross-language consumers against a test server that emits out-of-order seq numbers and simulated drops
Chaos tests: network flaps, 429 bursts, and slow consumers to validate backpressure enforcement
Performance benchmark harness: measure per-chunk CPU/latency for each language under default settings
Interop matrix: Python/TS/Go clients x runtime versions (stable, canary, legacy) automated in CI
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (canary): release SDK preview builds + feature-flagged server behavior to 5 internal teams for 2 weeks
Phase 2 (open beta): widen to external customers who opt-in via console feature flag; collect telemetry for 4 weeks
Phase 3 (GA): flip default to new contract, release stable SDK versions, publish migration guide
Fallback mechanism: server-side compatibility mode for 90 days post-GA where both old and new envelopes accepted
dependencies: runtime-team: streaming-envelope headers and deprecation flag
sdk-engineering: implement flow-control primitives per language
infra: CI matrix and test harness to run cross-language interop
docs: example apps and API reference pages
stakeholders: Eng leads: Mateo Lin (Python SDK), Sara Nguyen (TS SDK), Omar Haddad (Go SDK)
notes: Eng feedback (2026-03-11): prefer smaller default max_inflight for serverless customers; added label to make value configurable
Design decision: use opaque cursor tokens instead of structured offsets to allow future sharding changes
We opted for conservative retry defaults to avoid duplicate downstream side-effects reported in prior incidents
